content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with their planners and content experts, have disclosed that they have no financial interests or relationships with manufacturers of commercial products, suppliers of commercial services, or commercial supporters. The National Association of State Public Health Veterinarians (NASPHV) recognizes the positive benefits of human-animal interaction. While it is impossible to eliminate all risks associated with animal contact, this report provides recommendations to minimize the risk of disease and injury. NASPHV advises local and state public health, agricultural, environmental, and wildlife agencies to use these recommendations to establish their own guidelines or regulations to reduce the risk of disease transmission from human-animal contact in public settings. These settings include animal displays, petting zoos, animal swap meets, pet stores, zoological institutions, nature parks, circuses, carnivals, farm tours, livestock-birthing exhibits, county or state fairs, schools, and wildlife photo opportunities. Managers of these venues should utilize the information in this report to mitigate the risk of disease transmission. Although service animals (e.g., guide dogs) are not specifically addressed in this report, the general principles and recommendations are applicable to these settings. Public venues such as fairs, farm tours, petting zoos, and schools provide opportunities for entertainment and education. However, inadequate understanding of disease transmission and animal behavior can increase the likelihood of infectious diseases, rabies exposures, injuries, and other health problems among visitors, particularly children, in these settings. Zoonotic diseases, which are transmitted from animals to humans, are of particular concern, especially in cases where large numbers of people become ill. Since 1991, approximately 50 human infectious disease outbreaks involving animals in public settings have been reported to the CDC. These outbreaks have been associated with fairs and petting zoos. Reported outbreaks, diseases, or injuries attributed to human-animal interactions in public settings have prompted the solicitation of comments and suggestions from NASPHV members and questions from the public. In November 2006, NASPHV members and external expert consultants convened at the CDC in Atlanta, Georgia. The first day of the meeting was dedicated to reviewing scientific information regarding recent outbreaks, associated risk factors, pathogen biology, and interventional studies. A moderated discussion of each section of the recommendations was conducted. The committee reviewed scientific evidence and expert opinions in revising the document. A committee consensus was required to add or modify existing language or recommendations. Infections with enteric (intestinal) bacteria and parasites pose the highest risk for human disease from animals in public settings. Healthy animals can harbor human enteric pathogens, many of which have a low infectious dose. Due to the popularity of animal venues, a substantial number of people may be exposed. Illness and outbreaks of enteric diseases among visitors to fairs, farms, and petting zoos are well-documented. Pathogens responsible for outbreaks include Escherichia coli O157:H7 and other Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC), Campylobacter, Salmonella, and Cryptosporidium. Although cattle, sheep, or goats are often identified as sources of infection, poultry, rodents, and other domestic and wild animals are also potential sources. The primary mode of transmission for enteric pathogens is fecal-oral. Animal fur, hair, skin, and saliva can become contaminated with fecal organisms, leading to transmission when individuals pet, touch, feed, or are licked by animals. Illness has also been associated with contaminated clothing, shoes, animal bedding, flooring, barriers, and other environmental surfaces. Animals shedding pathogens such as STEC, Salmonella, and Campylobacter often exhibit no signs of illness and can intermittently shed these pathogens. Removing ill animals, especially those with diarrhea, is necessary but not sufficient to protect animal and human health. Healthy-appearing animals often shed pathogens that contaminate the environment. Some pathogens can survive for months or years in the environment. Multiple factors increase the probability of disease transmission at animal exhibits. Animals are more likely to shed pathogens due to stress induced by prolonged transportation, confinement, crowding, and increased handling by people. Commingling of animals increases the likelihood of pathogen transmission between animals. The prevalence of certain enteric pathogens is often higher in young animals, which are frequently used in petting zoos and educational programs. Shedding of STEC and Salmonella is highest in the summer and fall when many traveling animal exhibits, agricultural fairs, and petting zoos are scheduled. Certain human factors and behaviors, especially in children, increase the risk of infections. Children are particularly attracted to animal venues and are at increased risk for serious infections. The layout and maintenance of facilities and animal exhibits also affect the risk of infection. Risk factors include inadequate hand-washing facilities, structural deficiencies associated with temporary food-service facilities, inappropriate visitor flow, and incomplete separation between animal exhibits and food preparation and consumption areas. Contaminated or inadequately maintained drinking water and sewage or manure-disposal systems also contribute to the risk. Lessons from outbreaks have highlighted the importance of hand hygiene and environmental sanitation. For example, in 2000, two E. coli O157:H7 outbreaks in Pennsylvania and Washington prompted the CDC to establish recommendations for enteric disease prevention associated with farm animal contact. Risk factors identified in both outbreaks included direct animal contact and inadequate hand washing. In the Pennsylvania outbreak, 51 individuals, with a median age of 4 years, became ill within 10 days of visiting a dairy farm. Eight of these patients developed hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), a potentially fatal consequence of STEC infection. The same strain of E. coli O157:H7 was isolated from cattle, patients, and the farm environment. In another example, a 1996 Salmonella outbreak at a Colorado zoo was associated with touching a wooden barrier around a temporary Komodo dragon exhibit. Children who were not ill were significantly more likely to have washed their hands after visiting the exhibit. Salmonella was isolated from patients, a Komodo dragon, and the wooden barrier. Outbreaks have also occurred due to indirect contact with contaminated environments. For instance, in 2001, an Ohio outbreak of E. coli O157:H7 infections involved 23 individuals who became ill after handling sawdust, attending a dance, or eating and drinking in a barn where animals had been exhibited. Fourteen weeks after the fair, E. coli O157:H7 was isolated from multiple environmental sources within the barn, including sawdust on the floor and dust on the rafters. Injuries associated with animals in public settings include bites, kicks, falls, scratches, stings, crushing of the hands or feet, and being pinned between the animal and a fixed object. Rabies exposures have also occurred, requiring extensive public health investigation and medical follow-up. Although no human rabies deaths caused by animal contact in public exhibits have been recorded, thousands of individuals have received rabies postexposure prophylaxis (PEP) after exposure to rabid or potentially rabid animals. Other infections associated with animal contact include bacterial, viral, fungal, and parasitic agents. For example, ringworm outbreaks have been documented among individuals exhibiting lambs during show seasons. Zoonotic pathogens can also be transmitted through contact with reproductive fluids, aborted fetuses, or newborns from infected animals. Diseases such as Q fever, leptospirosis, listeriosis, brucellosis, and chlamydiosis can be acquired through contact with reproductive materials. Recommendations for local, state, and federal agencies include enhancing communication and cooperation among human and animal health agencies, conducting additional research into risk factors and prevention methods, and improving surveillance for health issues associated with animal contact. Education is essential to reduce risks associated with animal contact in public settings. Venue operators should be knowledgeable about the risks for disease and injury associated with animals and implement appropriate risk-reduction measures.
